_metadata.scope: Ancestor (above-item) divisions of Giles of Rome's Commentary on the Sentences (Gi9qrR); currently Liber 1 Prologus, Liber 1 Distinctio 37 (with Partes 1-2), Liber 2 Distinctio 44

Gi9qrR-d1e183.summary: Giles's Prologue to Book I treats theology itself as a science and then expounds the Lombard's own prologue. Its three questions analyze theology through its four causes. Question 1 (material cause, subject in itself) defines the subject of a science as its principal, formal object and concludes that theology is simpliciter a special science whose subject is God under the special ratio of restorer and glorifier, which distinguishes it from metaphysics, which treats God only as being and universal cause. Question 2 draws out what theology derives from that subject: order (subalternated to no human science but, analogically, to the science of God and the blessed, while all human sciences serve it as handmaids by reason of the end), dignity (above every human science, metaphysics included), unity (by the unity of its object, God), and necessity (non-superfluous, the one honorable science of wayfarers). Question 3 completes the scheme with the formal, efficient, and final causes: theology is properly wisdom rather than science and is simpliciter the most certain discipline though not the clearest; God alone teaches it in every way, angels and humans only instrumentally; and its principal end is charity, making it an affective science, more speculative than practical. The Expositio then reads the Lombard's prologue as a threefold commendation of the Sentences (dignity of matter, rationality of method through the four causes, utility), with deterrents to the work each overcome by an incentive rooted in charity. The literal Dubitationes settle verbal difficulties: inquiry into lofty things is licit when it relies on divine aid, expository additions to Scripture are legitimate, truth is hated only in its effects, and true words can be false relative to a deceptive intention.
claims: The subject of theology is God under the special ratio of restorer and glorifier, which makes theology a special science distinct from metaphysics.
Theology is subalternated to no human science but to the science of God and the blessed; all human sciences are subordinated to it by reason of the end.
Theology surpasses every human science in dignity and certitude and is one science by the unity of its object, God.
Theology is properly wisdom rather than science, taught by God alone in every way, and ordered principally to charity as an affective science.
The Lombard's prologue commends the Sentences by the dignity of its matter, the rationality of its method, and its utility.

Gi9qrR-d1e5722.summary: Distinction 37, Part 1 treats God's existence in things. The Prooemium divides the Lombard's text: God's omnipresence as distinct from creatures' local, mobile presence; the general modes (essence, presence, power) and special modes (grace, union, adoption); saints compared with sinners; and the closing questions on where God dwelt before creation and on his immunity from contamination. Question 1 shows that God is really present in created things by reason of his causality of being, his spirituality, immensity, and power. This presence divides into three general modes grounded in creation and two special modes (grace of union, grace of adoption) grounded in re-creation, and God alone is also 'in himself' in a fourfold sense. Question 2 shows that God is everywhere as the present container and conserver of all places and times, not as a body occupying space. Such per se ubiquity is proper to God alone, any apparent ubiquity of creatures being accidental. It is eternal as absoluteness from determination and as universal presence, but God's actual presence in created things is a temporal relation, whereas things' being in God is eternal. The Expositio litterae glosses the Lombard's wording: the wicked are where God is without being 'with' him, speech and understanding diverge in matters of faith, God's presence in place is essential and not merely causal, and acting on impurity does not entail being contaminated by it.
claims: God is really present in all things by his causality, spirituality, immensity, and power, according to three general and two special modes.
Per se ubiquity belongs to God alone; any creaturely ubiquity is accidental.
Things' being in God is eternal, while God's being in created things is a temporal relation.
God's presence in place is essential, not merely causal, and his contact with impure things does not contaminate him.
concepts: res in Deo vs. Deus in rebus

Gi9qrR-d1e5842.summary: Distinction 37, Part 2 moves from God's uncircumscribed presence to the place and motion of creatures, especially angels. The Prooemium divides the Lombard's argument that every creature, spiritual ones included, is place-defined and subject to variation, while God alone is uncircumscribed and immobile; it notes that the Lombard has digressed from the knowledge of God to God's existence in things. Question 1 (the place of angels) rests on one principle: an angel is in place not through its essence but by the operative application of its finite 'quantity of virtue' to a body. It follows that an angel is never simply nowhere, given the required connection of the universe; its place is extended but bounded and it is wholly present in each part; it cannot be in genuinely many places at once; and two angels cannot share one place, since all angels relate to place uniformly, unlike pairs related to a place in different ways (soul and body, God and creature). Question 2 (the motion of angels) holds that angels move in a qualified proper sense, grounded in the succession of their operations. They cannot pass between places without traversing the medium by application of virtue, and their motion is always measured by time. Giles allows that this time may be a discontinuous succession of instants, distinct from the continuous time of celestial motion, and treats the soul's departure at death along parallel lines. The Expositio litterae glosses Augustine's denial of dimensive quantity in God and the analogy of wisdom wholly present in each wise man, by which God is wholly in each thing.
claims: An angel is in place through the operation of its finite virtue on a body, not through its essence.
Because all angels relate to place uniformly, one angel cannot be in many places, and two angels cannot be in one place.
Angels move in a qualified proper sense, grounded in the succession of their operations, and must traverse the intervening medium.
Angelic motion is always measured by time, which may be a discontinuous succession of instants distinct from continuous celestial time.
God alone is uncircumscribed and immobile, existing wholly and undivided in each thing without dimensive quantity.

Gi9qrR-d1e5717.summary: Distinction 37 of Book I treats how God and creatures are in things and in place, set out as a contrast between God's unlimited presence and creatures' limited location. Part 1 establishes that God is really present in all things by his causality, spirituality, immensity, and power. This presence comes in three general modes (presence, power, essence) and two special modes (grace of union, grace of adoption), and God alone is also 'in himself' in a fourfold sense. His ubiquity is per se and proper to him alone, though his actual presence in created things is a temporal relation while things' being in him is eternal. Part 2 turns to creatures, which are all place-defined and mutable, and works out angelic location and motion from one principle. An angel is in place by the operative application of its finite virtue, not by its essence. It therefore cannot be in many places at once or share its place with another angel. It moves in a qualified proper sense, must traverse the intervening medium, and is measured by a time that may be a discontinuous succession of instants. Literal glosses in both parts defend God's essential (not merely causal) presence, his immunity from contamination, and his undivided presence in each thing without dimensive quantity. Across the distinction Giles draws a single contrast: God's presence follows from infinite power and is unbounded, while a creature's location follows from finite power and is bounded.
claims: God is really, essentially, and per se present in all things by three general and two special modes, and ubiquity belongs to God alone.
Creatures, including angels, are place-defined and mutable, while God alone is uncircumscribed and immobile.
An angel is in place and moves by the operation of its finite virtue, which excludes multilocation and the co-location of two angels.
Angelic motion is measured by time, possibly a discontinuous time distinct from celestial time.

Gi9qrR-dm9880.summary: Distinction 44, the last distinction of Book II, treats the power to sin and obedience. The Praeambulum divides the Lombard's text into three parts: whether the power to sin comes from God, the devil, or man (resolved in favor of God); whether power so derived must always be obeyed; and the transition to Book III, with an overview of the order of all four books. Question 1 (on the power to sin) argues that this power, as a being and as identical with free will, is from God, though the sinful act and the abuse of the power are not. It extends this to all rulership, which comes from God as efficient and final cause even when it is wrongly acquired or used. Rulership would also have existed without the Fall in a directive, non-despotic form (political and paternal rule, and dominion over animals), whereas the despotic and corrective rule of man over man results from sin. Question 2 (on obedience) holds that obedience is a special virtue, formally part of justice, though materially it can perform the acts of every virtue. The faithful owe obedience even to unbelieving lords whose rule is just, since Christian liberty is spiritual. A professed religious owes strict obedience to his prelate only within the matters of his rule and never against divine or natural law. A dubitatio on hierarchical obedience and literal glosses close Book II. Both questions rely on the same Augustinian distinction: a power or order is from God as being, but not as defect, abuse, or consequence of sin.
claims: The power to sin, as a being and as free will, is from God, though the sinful act and its abuse are not.
All rulership is from God as efficient and final cause; its corrupt acquisition and use are not.
Directive, non-despotic rule would have existed in the state of innocence, while despotic and corrective rule of man over man results from sin.
Obedience is a special virtue and part of justice, owed to just rulers whether believers or not, and for religious bounded by their rule and by divine and natural law.
